title: From Uncontrolled Variables to Quantifiable Execution: Rethinking the Pavlik Philosophy Through Rehabilitation Engineering
content: The Pavlik harness works remarkably well for babies under six months and about 8 to 10 kg. Outside that window, clinicians do not use it, and for good reason. But why exactly that boundary exists has never been fully explained in biomechanical terms. This article argues that Pavlik's control-theoretic idea, soft constraint plus bounded autonomous movement, is not the problem. The problem is that both of its inputs get scrambled by variables no one currently measures: body weight, limb dimensions, muscle strength, tone, developmental stage. These variables modulate the actual mechanical environment so heavily that identical strap settings produce wildly different outcomes across patients. Clinics respond by retreating to a narrow age window. We think there is another way: measure those variables, compensate for them, and see how far the Pavlik philosophy can actually reach. We lay out four research questions under a working label, CMVDF or Controllable Motion-Variable Dynamic Fixation, place everything squarely inside the IHDI safety framework, and sketch speculative extensions to CP and SMA. This is a research agenda. It is not a clinical protocol.
